Direct, Convergent α‑Amidation of β‑Keto Esters via Nickelocene
Catalysis
Kimberly R. Sharp, Sara Y. Siddiqui, Emily G. Nikas, and Brian M. Stoltz*

Cite This: Org. Lett. 2025, 27, 6380−6384

ABSTRACT: α-Amidation of carbonyl-containing compounds
without prefunctionalization of starting materials represents a
continuing challenge within the scientific community. Here,
nickelocene is used catalytically to effect an amidation of β-keto
esters. Broad substrate tolerance on both coupling partners is
achieved, enabling the application toward a convergent synthetic
strategy. Initial mechanistic investigations suggest complex
activation pathways.
N

itrogen functionality α to carbonyl groups, beyond the
20 naturally occurring amino acids, is found in many
natural products and pharmacologically active materials
(Figure 1A).1,2 To enable a desirable synthetic strategy for
access to this class of compounds, introduction of an amine or
amide functionality at a late stage may be appealing. However,
most methods to do so currently rely on either prefunction-
alization of the carbonyl moiety3 or require introducing
nitrogen in a higher oxidation state,4 subsequently necessitat-
ing reduction and lengthening a synthetic sequence. Avoiding
this additional manipulation through the development of
methods to directly amidate unfunctionalized carbonyl-
containing compounds is thus of importance to the synthetic
community.

Advances have been made in the area of α-amination, with
examples utilizing both transition metal catalysis and
biocatalysis, although these strategies struggle to accommodate
electron-withdrawing substituents.5 Recent advances over-
coming this challenge have enabled the incorporation of
carbamates and N-tosylates by leveraging active intermediates,
such as nitrenes,6,7 N-centered radicals,8 or reaction with α-
oxidized carbonyl compounds.9 While these methods all
represent key advances in the strategy for the direct
introduction of nitrogen α to carbonyls, further sequential
transformations would be necessary to introduce complexity
on the nitrogen moiety. In an ideal convergent coupling
strategy, a functionalized amide could be brought in directly,
forging this key bond in a more advantageous fashion for
synthetic efficiency (Figure 1B).

To this end, methodology has been disclosed by the groups
of Yu and Bao,10 Zong, Jiang, and Qiu,11 and Chang12 using
iron catalysis, which in conjunction with photochemistry can
achieve α-amidation (Figure 1C). This reaction manifold,
however, suffers from challenges, largely revolving around
sterics at the α position; either reactivity is limited when α
substitution is included, or α substitution is needed to prevent

double amidation. Additionally, a broad substrate tolerance on
both coupling partners was a challenge in all reports. As a
result, an alternate catalytic system allowing for selective yet
reactive amidation is thus desirable. Here, we demonstrate a
system capable of achieving selective amidation of β-keto esters
with broad functional group tolerance on both coupling
partners (Figure 1D).

We began our investigations by turning to a previous report
from our group in which we leveraged a proposed nitrene
intermediate as an electrophilic amide source for the synthesis
of hydrazides.13 We hypothesized that trapping this inter-
mediate with an enolate would forge the desired bond under
nickel catalysis. In an effort to develop a reaction capable of
forming fully substituted carbon centers, the reactivity between
ethyl 2-methyl-3-oxobutanoate (1a) and N-(benzoyloxy)-
benzamide (2a) was explored. To our delight, the initial
investigation using nickel half-sandwich catalyst14 4a and
lithium tert-butoxide as a base resulted in the formation of the
desired amidated product 3a, albeit in a low yield (Table 1,
entry 1). Reinvestigation of half-sandwich catalysts revealed
that compound 4b, with bulkier NHC substitution, improved
the yield to 36% (entry 2). The solvent mixture of
dichloromethane and tetrahydrofuran (THF), while vital for
achieving high yields in previous nickel chemistry,13 was no
longer optimal in this system, and 1,4-dioxane was found to
both improve the yield and reaction time (entry 4). Alternate
bases were investigated (entries 5 and 6), although lithium tert-
butoxide remained optimal. Interestingly, a counterion effect

was observed for the base, with potassium tert-butoxide failing
to generate more than a small amount of product. Alternate
silane reductants were explored (entries 7 and 8), although
phenylsilane proved superior. Further investigation of
additives, including equivalents of silane,15 can be found in
the Supporting Information.

At this stage, a few general reaction mechanisms were
explored. To examine if this reaction proceeds through an
uncatalyzed SN2 reaction at nitrogen, precedented for alternate
N−O species,16 the catalyst was omitted (entry 9). As no
product was observed in the absence of a nickel catalyst, this
pathway was rejected. The possibility of nickel acting as a
Lewis acid to activate the starting materials was also explored;
replacing the nickel catalyst with catalytic amounts of a variety
of Lewis acids resulted in no product formation (see the
Supporting Information), leading to nickel catalysis being
favored as the most likely manifold.

Further mechanistic analysis revealed key differences
between this transformation and our previous report on the
nickel-catalyzed synthesis of hydrazides.13 Previously, a Ni(I)
active catalyst was proposed, with the role of phenylsilane

hypothesized to be reduction of the Ni(II) precatalyst.17 In the
current study, however, upon preparing Ni(I) catalyst 4c and
subjecting it to reaction conditions in the absence of
phenylsilane, no reaction was observed (entry 10). Addition-
ally, throughout the optimization of this amidation reaction,
side products analogous to compound 5 were observed,18

presumed to arise through a deleterious side reaction between
the starting material and catalyst. Despite this use of the same
hydroxamic ester and catalyst in our previous report,13 these
side products were never observed, further suggesting
mechanistic divergence.

Following several unsuccessful attempts to induce enantio-
selectivity through the inclusion of asymmetric ligands, we
began to consider the possibility of off-metal redox activation.
We were drawn to previous reports suggesting that ferrocene is
capable of N−O bond cleavage through single-electron transfer
from ferrocene, generating imidyl19 and amidyl20 radicals, as
well as a precedent for amidyl radicals as intermediates in α
amidation.8,10 As metallocene catalysts were an appealing
alternative to avoid the observed NHC−hydroxamate adduct
(5), nickelocene was investigated for its competence in the
reaction. Gratifyingly, nickelocene led to similar yields (Table
2, entry 1), with lower catalyst loadings now preferred (entry
2). Notably, in comparison to half-sandwich catalysis, markedly
shorter reaction times were observed for other β-keto ester
substrates (Supporting Information). Decreasing the base
loading slightly and increasing the temperature led to a now
optimal 82% yield (entry 3); performing this reaction on a 1.0
mmol scale led to a similar yield of 78% (entry 4),
demonstrating good scalability. Furthermore, while ferrocene
and cobaltocene both led to product formation, they were
slower and less effective than nickelocene (entries 5 and 6).
This represents a rare example of nickelocene in catalysis,
despite its longstanding study in inorganic chemistry literature.

The scope of the reaction was then investigated (Scheme 1).
The α substituent could be replaced with an ethyl with no
decrease in the yield observed (3b). β-Keto esters with no α-
substitution also performed well (3c and 3d), with good yields

of the singly amidated product. Aryl β-keto esters also formed
the product in a high yield (3e). Inclusion of a chiral auxiliary
resulted in product formation with some diastereocontrol (3f).
Cyclic β-keto esters also performed well, with 5- through 7-
membered rings resulting in good yields (3g−3i). While both
were electronically differentiated from the standard material, β-

keto amides (3j) and malonates (3k and 3l) were competent
in the reaction.

On the hydroxamate starting material, electron-donating and
electron-withdrawing substituents could be added with little
impact on the yield (6a−6c). Substitution including halogens,
either p-Cl (6d) or p-CF3 (6e), did lead to a decrease, though
good yields were still produced. Styrenyl substitution could
additionally be included (6f), with no competing side reactivity
observed. Alkenyl and aliphatic substituents were also
competent in the reaction (6g−6l). Notably, benzyl sub-
stitution (6h) is well-tolerated in this reaction, contrasting with
our group’s previous report where the starting material was
inert to reaction conditions13 as well as further indicating
selectivity against benzylic functionalization. Cyclic alkyl
substituents displayed a dependence on ring sizes, with smaller
cyclopropyl hydroxamates outperforming cyclopentyl (6j and
6k) (vide infra).
To further investigate the mechanism of this reaction, we
explored two main reaction manifolds proposed for prior iron-
catalyzed transformations, either a nitrene pathway11,12 or a
radical pathway.10 Beginning by exposing the reaction
conditions to triphenylphosphine to intercept a potential
nitrene intermediate (Scheme 2A), different outcomes were
observed depending on the inclusion or exclusion of β-keto
ester 1a. In the absence of compound 1a, no iminophosphor-

ane 7 was observed, although upon inclusion of β-keto ester
1a, compound 7 was formed in 18% yield, alongside a small
amount of amidated product 3a. This contrasting activity may
suggest a role for the β-keto ester in the formation of a reactive
nitrogen species. Additionally, while the formation of an
iminophosphorane is traditionally associated with trapping of
an active nitrene intermediate,21 a recently proposed
mechanism for its formation involves interception of a N-
centered radical with phosphorus, followed by oxidation,22

suggesting that the formation of this side product is
inconclusive.

In an attempt to trap a key radical intermediate, TEMPO
was included in the reaction conditions (Scheme 2B). While
the resulting species was too unstable for isolation, the mass of
the potential TEMPO adduct formed with a N-centered radical
originating from hydroxamate 2a was observed via high-
resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) analysis. These experi-
ments taken alongside precedented analogous reactivity with
ferrocene led us to hypothesize the intermediacy of a N-
centered radical species. Such an intermediate would also
suggest an explanation for the different outcomes observed for
the formation of compounds 6i and 6j vs compound 6k, as the
cyclopentyl substrate is large enough to potentially undergo a
deleterious 1,5-hydrogen atom transfer inaccessible to either
the isopropyl or cyclopropyl starting materials.

In conclusion, we have developed a nickel-catalyzed
amidation of β-keto esters, enabling the convenient and
convergent synthesis of α-amidated materials. Both aliphatic
and aromatic substituents are well-tolerated on either coupling
partner. The use of nickelocene in catalysis is disclosed, with
favorable reactivity in comparison to other metallocenes. A N-
centered radical is hypothesized as a reactive intermediate from
the initial mechanistic investigation. Further experimental and
computational investigations into the mechanism are ongoing.
